source.title: Languages You Know Influence Those You Learn: Impact of Language Characteristics on Multi-Lingual Text-to-Text Transfer
source.authors: Benjamin Muller; Deepanshu Gupta; Siddharth Patwardhan; J. Fauconnier; David Vandyke; Sachin Agarwal

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether downstream task performance can be predicted from language-model performance, using multilingual transfer measurements and regression rather than a scale sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior language-model scaling work but does not test parameter, token, or compute scaling laws. Its own relevant results are correlations and regressions linking masked-span language-model metrics to downstream cross-lingual task performance. Other reported predictors and few-shot sample-count results are outside the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. but runs no scale sweep. It uses one model (mT5 base) and correlates per-language masked-span LM metrics with cross-lingual transfer across language pairs. V6 concerns downstream gains with model scale or pretraining loss across models or checkpoints. Variation across languages inside one fixed model is a related but different construct. The bivariate correlations also target the transfer gap (ST−SS), not downstream performance itself. Findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right; it omits the paper's headline findings. The authors conclude that cross-lingual transfer in mT5 base can be modelled by a few linguistic and data-derived features. Syntactic, morphological and phonological similarity predict transfer better than lexical similarity. Target-language LM performance is an informative predictor in the multivariate model, although its bivariate correlations are counter-intuitive (negative for QA). Few-shot performance rises roughly logarithmically with the number of target samples.
record.recipe_differences: This is a multilingual transfer-prediction analysis, not a parameter/token/compute scaling-law measurement or compute-optimal allocation study.
record.method_sensitivity: The bivariate language-model associations differ across tasks and between source- and target-language measures; multivariate feature selection yields positive target-language LMEM coefficients across all three tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Within mT5 base, per-language masked-span LM metrics correlate with zero-shot cross-lingual transfer gap inconsistently in sign and significance across tasks (Table 1). Target-language LM exact-match accuracy gets a positive significant coefficient in the multivariate zero-shot regressions for QA, NER and XNLI (Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a fixed multilingual model, a language's pretraining-objective performance predicts downstream cross-lingual task performance for that language.

fits_no_version.finding: Few-shot target-language performance correlates most strongly with log(n) of target fine-tuning samples for QA (83.9) and NER (69.0); for XNLI, log²(n) correlates best and only weakly (18.0) (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual few-shot fine-tuning performance grows roughly log-linearly in the number of target-language examples.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to mT5 base, three downstream tasks, and the studied languages. The LM metrics are predictors in observational correlations/regressions, not interventions; the reported cross-validation RMSE is for the full selected-feature models, so it does not isolate the predictive contribution of the LM metric. No model-scale or pretraining-loss scaling sweep is performed.

untested.parts: No parameter, token or compute sweep; no pretraining loss curve.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No power-law fit in another regime. The few-shot sample curve is log-linear fine-tuning performance in one model, not a scaling-law test.
No variation in model scale or pretraining loss across models or checkpoints; only one mT5 base model is studied.

missing.what: Pearson correlations of target performance with n, log(n) and log²(n) of few-shot target samples per task.
n-shot meta-regression RMSE (QA 5.69, NER 7.60, XNLI 8.13), and the statement that the LM-metric influence dies out as target samples grow.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link conflates within-model, across-language predictors with the scale-or-loss predictability that V6 names. Table 1 as printed shows identical MORPH and Vr columns (-40.7, -2.4, 10.8), possibly an extraction or typesetting error; this does not affect the rows. The bivariate correlations use ST−SS as the target; the regressions use ST(0).

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over parameter count, training tokens, or compute; no held-out pretraining-loss scaling analysis.
No prediction of much larger runs from smaller runs.
No comparison of model architecture dimensions at fixed parameter count.
No tests of the scaling-law form across modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream performance prediction using masked-span language-model metrics in multilingual transfer; does not test prediction from model scale or a pretraining-loss scaling curve.
Does not examine scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, or their sensitivity to fitting choices.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Bivariate correlations between language-model metrics and cross-lingual transfer gap across tasks and source/target sides
reader_labels.reason: Associations vary by task and metric; several are not significant and significant correlations include negative directions, so the simple relationship is not consistent (r1–r12).
